text: The Aegean Sea is an elongated embayment of the Mediterranean Sea situated between Europe and Asia, located between the Balkans and Anatolia, covering an area of approximately 214,000 square kilometres (83,000 sq mi), measuring about 670 kilometres (420 mi) longitudinally and 390 kilometres (240 mi) latitudinally. It reaches a maximum depth of 2,639 metres (8,658 ft) west of Karpathos and is bordered on the south by islands including Kythera, Antikythera, Crete, Kasos, Karpathos, and Rhodes, with the Anatolian peninsula marking its eastern boundary and the Greek mainland its western boundary. The sea contains several subdivisions, including the Thracian Sea to the north, the Icarian Sea to the east, the Myrtoan Sea to the west, and the Sea of Crete to the south. The Aegean Islands, which are mostly part of Greece, are divided into groups such as the Dodecanese (including Rhodes, Kos, and Patmos), the Cyclades (including Delos and Naxos), the Sporades, the Saronic islands, the North Aegean Islands (including Lesbos), and Crete and its surrounding islands. Many of these island chains are geographical extensions of the mainland mountains, extending to Chios, Samos, and Rhodes. The sea is connected to the Marmara Sea via the Dardanelles (known as the Hellespont in Classical Antiquity), which in turn connects to the Black Sea through the Bosporus strait, upon which lies Istanbul. The Turkish Straits comprise the Dardanelles and the Bosporus. The Aegean's physical oceanography is influenced by the regional climate, freshwater discharge from rivers, and seasonal variations in Black Sea outflow through the Dardanelles, with surface water circulating in a counterclockwise gyre. Hypersaline Mediterranean water moves northward along Turkey’s west coast, sinks below Black Sea outflow at 23–30 metres (75–98 ft), flows through the Dardanelles at 5–15 cm/s (2–6 in/s), and then moves westward along the northern Aegean before flowing southward along Greece’s east coast. The climate is predominantly Mediterranean (Csa) in most areas, with hotter, drier summers and milder, wetter winters, while the northern regions have a Cold semi-arid (BSk) climate. The Etesian winds are a dominant weather influence. Major cities along the coast include Athens, Thessaloniki, Volos, Kavala, Heraklion in Greece, and İzmir and Bodrum in Turkey. Crete is the most populated Aegean island, followed by Euboea and Rhodes. The Aegean has historically been significant to Ancient Greece, hosting the Minoan civilization (flourishing from 3000 to 1450 BC, ending around 1100 BC) on Crete and the Mycenaean civilization (1600–1100 BC) on the mainland, both of which contributed to the term "Aegean civilization." The Minoans developed extensive trade networks and built large palaces such as Knossos and Phaistos, while the Mycenaeans established a warrior elite society centered on palace states, used the Linear B script, and developed military and architectural innovations. The collapse of the Mycenaean civilization led to the Greek Dark Ages, during which writing ceased and trade declined. The Archaic period (8th century BC) saw the rise of independent city-states like Athens, Sparta, and Corinth, which became maritime powers, and the establishment of the Greek alphabet from the Phoenician script. The Battle of Salamis in 480 BC, where the Athenian fleet defeated the Persian fleet under Xerxes II, was a pivotal naval engagement. The Aegean later came under the control of the Kingdom of Macedonia, with Philip II and Alexander the Great achieving dominance, followed by the Hellenistic period after Alexander’s death, with Cassander ruling western Greece and Lysimachus controlling the eastern coast. The Roman Republic, through the Macedonian Wars, gained control over the eastern Mediterranean, including the Aegean, and established provinces such as Achaea, Macedonia, Thracia, Asia, and Creta et Cyrenaica. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the Byzantine Empire maintained control over the Aegean, though it faced threats from early Muslim conquests, including the Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates. In the 820s, Crete was conquered by Berber Andalusian exiles and became an independent Islamic emirate, which remained a major threat to Byzantium for about 135 years, serving as a base for Muslim corsairs. The Byzantines retook Crete under Nikephoros II Phokas in 960–961. The Bulgarian Empire also threatened Byzantine control, with Presian, Boris I, Simeon I, and Ivan Asen II expanding into northern and western Aegean coasts. The Seljuk Turks invaded in 1068, annexing Anatolian territories including the eastern Aegean coast, and later the Sultanate of Rum took control. The Byzantines regained the eastern coast. Following the Fourth Crusade, the Aegean was fragmented into entities such as the Latin Empire, the Kingdom of Thessalonica, the Empire of Nicaea, and the Principality of Achaea. Greece has established several marine protected areas, including Alonnisos Marine Park, and four Greek MPAs are part of the MedPAN network. The current coastline dates back to about 4000 BC, with the northern Aegean previously being large coastal plains during the last ice age, when sea levels were 130 metres (430 ft) lower; the present configuration emerged around 9,000 years ago as sea levels rose. The sea was known as Mare Aegaeum in Latin and as Archipelago in Greek, with the Turkish name Ege Denizi derived from the Greek name and Adalar Denizi meaning "Sea of Islands." In some South Slavic languages, it is called White Sea (Bulgarian: Byalo more, Macedonian: Belo more, Serbian: Belo more). Sovereignty issues between Greece and Turkey, including territorial waters, national airspace, exclusive economic zones, and flight information regions, have significantly affected Greece-Turkey relations since the 1970s. The name Aegaeus, used by Late Latin authors, refers to Aegeus, the father of Theseus, who is said to have jumped into the sea to drown himself after believing his son had died upon returning from slaying the Minotaur, having forgotten to hoist white sails as instructed. The Aegean Sea is also known in some South Slavic languages as the White Sea, and its Turkish name is Ege Denizi.

Simeon I of Bulgaria led Bulgaria to its greatest territorial expansion, conquering much of the northern and western coasts of the Aegean Sea, though the Byzantines later regained control. The Second Bulgarian Empire achieved similar gains along the northern and western Aegean coasts under Ivan Asen II. The Seljuk Turks, under the Seljuk Empire, invaded the Byzantine Empire in 1068 and annexed almost all of Anatolia, including the east coast of the Aegean Sea, during the reign of Alp Arslan, the second Sultan of the Seljuk Empire. After Alp Arslan’s successor, Malik Shah I, died, the empire was divided, and Kilij Arslan I succeeded in Anatolia, founding the Sultanate of Rum. The Byzantines then recaptured the eastern coast of the Aegean. Following the occupation of Constantinople by Western European and Venetian forces during the Fourth Crusade, the Aegean area fragmented into the Latin Empire, the Kingdom of Thessalonica, the Empire of Nicaea, the Principality of Achaea, and the Duchy of Athens. The Venetians established the maritime state of the Duchy of the Archipelago, which included all the Cyclades except Mykonos and Tinos. The Empire of Nicaea, a Byzantine rump state, successfully recaptured Constantinople from the Latins in 1261 and defeated Epirus. However, Byzantine successes were short-lived; the Ottomans eventually conquered the Aegean coast, though the Byzantine Empire had already been weakened by internal conflicts. By the late 14th century, the Byzantines lost all control of the Aegean coast and could only exert influence around Constantinople. The Ottomans gained control of all the Aegean coast except Crete, which remained a Venetian colony until 1669. The Greek War of Independence enabled a Greek state on the Aegean coast from 1829 onward. After the Balkan Wars (1912–1913), Greece expanded northward along the coast, while Bulgaria gained access to the northernmost section. The Ottoman Empire maintained a presence over the Aegean for over 500 years until its dissolution after World War I, when it was replaced by modern Turkey. Following the war, Greece gained control of the northern Aegean coast, including territory previously held by Bulgaria. By the 1920s, Greece and Turkey had settled into their present-day borders. In the Italo-Turkish War of 1912, Italy captured the Dodecanese islands and has occupied them since, violating the 1919 Venizelos–Tittoni agreement to cede them to Greece. The Greco-Italian War occurred from October 1940 to April 1941 as part of the Balkans Campaign in World War II, with Italy aiming to establish a Greek puppet state to allow the annexation of the Sporades and Cyclades islands as part of the Italian Aegean Islands. The German invasion led to the Axis occupation of Greece; German troops evacuated Athens on 12 October 1944, and by the end of the month, they had withdrawn from mainland Greece. Greece was then liberated by Allied forces. Many Aegean islands have safe harbours and bays; in ancient times, sea navigation was easier than travel across the rugged terrain of the Greek mainland or coastal Anatolia. Many islands are volcanic, and marble and iron are mined on others. Larger islands have fertile valleys and plains. Of the main Aegean islands, two belong to Turkey—Bozcaada (Tenedos) and Gökçeada (Imbros); the rest belong to Greece. Political disputes between Greece and Turkey over territorial waters, air control, and economic rights to the continental shelf are known as the Aegean dispute. Multiple ports are located along the Greek and Turkish coasts. Piraeus in Athens is Greece’s chief port, the largest passenger port in Europe and the third largest in the world, serving about 20 million passengers annually. With a throughput of 1.4 million TEUs, Piraeus ranks among the top ten container ports in Europe and is the top container port in the Eastern Mediterranean. It is also Greece’s commercial hub for shipping and bi-annually hosts the Posidonia shipping convention. Piraeus is Greece’s third-busiest port in terms of goods transported, behind Agioi Theodoroi and Thessaloniki. The port serves ferry routes to nearly every island in eastern Greece, Crete, the Cyclades, the Dodecanese, and much of the northern and eastern Aegean, while its western section handles cargo. As of 2007, the Port of Thessaloniki was Greece’s second-largest container port, handling 14,373,245 tonnes of cargo and 222,824 TEUs. Paloukia on Salamis is a major passenger port. Fish is Greece’s second-largest agricultural export, and Greece has Europe’s largest fishing fleet. Catches include sardines, mackerel, grouper, grey mullets, sea bass, and seabream. Pelagic fisheries show dominant catches of anchovy in the north, horse mackerels in the center, and boops in the south; demersal fisheries show grey mullets in the north and pickerel (Spicara smaris) in the south. The industry was affected by the Great Recession, and overfishing and habitat destruction threaten grouper and seabream populations, possibly reducing fish catch by 50%. The Greek government has offered compensation to fishermen. Some species are protected under EU law, but illegal species such as Pinna nobilis, Charonia tritonis, and Lithophaga lithophaga are still sold in Greek restaurants and markets. The Aegean islands are major tourist destinations, contributing significantly to Greece’s tourism, especially since the second half of the 20th century. Five UNESCO World Heritage sites are located in the Aegean Islands: the Monastery of Saint John the Theologian and the Cave of the Apocalypse on Patmos, the Pythagoreion and Heraion of Samos, the Nea Moni of Chios, Delos, and the Medieval City of Rhodes. Greece is one of the most visited countries in Europe and the world, with over 33 million visitors in 2018, and tourism accounts for a quarter of Greece’s Gross Domestic Product. Common tourist destinations include Santorini, Crete, Lesbos, Delos, and Mykonos, with an estimated 2 million tourists visiting Santorini annually. Overtourism concerns have emerged, including inadequate infrastructure and overcrowding. Turkey has also developed resort areas and attracted large numbers of tourists, contributing to its tourism industry. The phrase "Blue Cruise" refers to recreational voyages along the Turkish Riviera, including across the Aegean. The ancient city of Troy, a World Heritage Site, lies on the Turkish coast of the Aegean. Greece and Turkey both participate in the Blue Flag beach certification program of the Foundation for Environmental Education, awarded for environmental protection, water quality, safety, and services. As of 2015, 395 beaches and 9 marinas in Greece held the Blue Flag. On the Turkish coast, southern Aegean beaches in Muğla (102), İzmir (49), and Aydın (30) received the certification.
